header:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-18
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Ethan Li (Redwood SE), Priya Menon (CTO - Orchid), Jonas Ortega (Platform Eng), Marta Ruiz (Head of Compliance)
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samira from Redwood, and with me is Ethan, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya: Doing good, thanks. We got a packed agenda, primarily around how you handle partial outages and what graceful degradation looks like.
[00:12] Ethan: Great, that's right up our alley. To be clear up front, we'd like to cover: routing, fallback model variants, multi-region failover, and the SLA semantics. Sound good?
[00:20] Jonas: Yep. Also Marta's going to ping in some compliance questions as we go.
[00:24] Marta: Hi, quick note — we'll need to understand the audit trail and key management. KMS integration is non-negotiable for us.
[00:30] Ethan: Understood. Quick context question: what's the current deployment style for your inference workloads? Hosted? On-prem? Hybrid?
[00:36] Priya: We are mainly on a hybrid pipeline. Inference for some non-sensitive features runs in a managed cloud, but PII-adjacent models must be kept in our VPC. We're evaluating Dedicated or Private for that.
[00:44] Samira: Makes sense. For clarity, Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with isolation; Private is a customer-managed control plane option. Both support our routing and fallbacks, but the toggles differ slightly.
[00:54] Jonas: Two immediate worries: tail latency during peak loads and when a whole AZ goes flakey. We need deterministic answers: what falls back to what, and how much latency do we add?
[01:02] Ethan: Good call. Our typical pattern is policy-driven routing. Primary -> regional replicas -> compatible model variant (lower cost/quantized) -> global fallback. Each hop adds measurable delta: regional replica is usually negligible, model variant might add 10-50ms decode variance, global fallback can add ~100-200ms depending on route+cold start.
[01:18] Priya: When you say cold start, is that for model loading on a cold node or for spinning up new nodes?
[01:22] Ethan: Both. Cold start is mostly model loading into GPU memory. We do warm pools and pre-warmed quantized variants for common sequences to reduce that, but worst-case first request can see a few hundred ms.
[01:30] Jonas: That's too high for some latency critical endpoints. Can we do a read-only lightweight fallback — like cached responses or embeddings only — to preserve latency SLA?
[01:38] Samira: Yes. We recommend a tiered fallback plan: prefix caching (for repeated prompts), short TTL cached responses, and a reduced feature set endpoint that returns embeddings or truncated completions. That reduces perceived latency and risk.
[01:48] Marta: From a compliance perspective, we need to ensure cached data is encrypted and has TTL logs. Also, eviction logs must be auditable.
[01:54] Ethan: We log cache hits/misses and eviction events in the audit trail. In Dedicated and Private deployments, logs can be forwarded to your SIEM; keys can be customer-managed via KMS/HSM.
[02:04] Priya: How do you express fallbacks? Is it in the API call or in console policies?
[02:09] Ethan: You can do both. There's policy DSL in the console for routing and fallback chains, and you can override per-request via headers to signal latency/quality preference.
[02:17] Jonas: Real world question: suppose us-east-1 has a networking blip. Traffic should fail over to us-west-2. How fast is that switchover, and is it per-request or session?
[02:26] Ethan: Failover is per-request by default. Agents will try primary, then fail to regional replica, then to fallback region. DNS/TCP layer health checks can route client traffic faster if you pair with our region-aware edge. Typical failover on application layer is sub-second after detecting retries, but end-to-end depends on client retry logic.
[02:38] Priya: Okay. For our SLA contracting, we need clear SLO numbers. What SLAs do you offer for Hosted vs Dedicated?
[02:44] Samira: Hosted has a standard 99.9% uptime SLA for API availability; Dedicated can go to 99.95% with reserved capacity and proactive capacity replacement. Private SLAs are negotiated since you're operating control plane elements.
[02:56] Marta: And how about credits? How does your credit mechanism work for degraded performance vs full outage?
[03:00] Samira: Credits are proportional to the duration and severity. For partial degradations we'd evaluate the impact on latency SLOs; the contract defines thresholds. We'll send a sample SLA schedule in the follow-up.
[03:08] Jonas: Are there built-in rate-limit backstops when a region is degraded to prevent cascading overload?
[03:12] Ethan: Yes, we support global and per-token throttles with dynamic shedding. You can set soft-limits and hard-limits and configure overflow policies: queue, reject, or route to cheaper variants.
[03:21] Priya: And if we route to a cheaper variant, how do we measure quality regressions? We need a signal to escalate to human review.
[03:27] Ethan: Good point. We emit per-response quality metadata — e.g., model_variant, quantization_level, confidence heuristics — and you can configure evaluators to run on a sample stream and raise alerts on regressions.
[03:36] Samira: This pairs with Redwood Optimize — it suggests quantization tiers by workload and flags regressions tied to prompt sets.
[03:42] Marta: On encryption, we require envelope encryption with our KMS; keys must never be exported. Is that supported?
[03:47] Ethan: Yes, customer-managed KMS is supported. For Hosted, keys are in your cloud KMS and are used for envelope encryption; for Private, you manage the KMS inside your VPC. Keys are never exportable.
[03:55] Priya: For the audit trail, we need per-token tracing back to the request origin and masking rules for sensitive tokens. Can Redwood provide that?
[04:01] Ethan: We provide token-level trace logs with redaction hooks. You can configure PII scrubbers and retention. For sensitive contexts we recommend Private so logs never leave your environment, but we can do secure log forwarding from Dedicated as well.
[04:12] Jonas: Let's talk about testing. For our pilot, we want to simulate an AZ failure and measure: request success rate, 95/99 latency, fallback rate to lower-tier model, and error distribution.
[04:21] Samira: That's doable. Ethan, can we propose a POC plan that runs a regional failover test for 48 hours and collects those metrics?
[04:27] Ethan: Yep. Proposed metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, time-to-first-byte, model-variant switch percentage, cache hit ratio, and end-to-end error rate. We'll instrument with traces and share dashboards.
[04:36] Priya: What about cost? Routing to global fallback — do you bill at the full model rate? We need clarity for chargebacks.
[04:42] Samira: Billing follows the model variant used for inference. If you fall back to a quantized cheaper variant, you'll see lower per-token cost. There are egress/networking elements for cross-region failover that we separate in the billing line items. We'll include sample cost scenarios.
[04:55] Jonas: For Dedicated, how much buffer should we reserve to hit 99.95%? Is there guidance on headroom?
[05:00] Ethan: Depends on your request distribution; typical rule is 20-30% buffer for headroom plus autoscale policies. For spiky workloads we recommend burst pools and predictive autoscaling based on sequence length distribution.
[05:10] Priya: Two things Marta wants to confirm: SOC2 coverage for Dedicated, and whether you support SAML/SSO with SCIM provisioning for role-based access.
[05:16] Samira: Yes to both. Dedicated customers can get an enterprise SOC2 attestation copy and we support SAML SSO with SCIM for provisioning. We'll send the compliance pack.
[05:23] Marta: On retention: logs retention policy is important. We may need retention for up to 7 years for certain audits; can you accommodate that?
[05:29] Ethan: We can support long-term retention if logs are forwarded to your storage; we don't recommend keeping huge retention in our console, but forwarding to GCS/S3 with lifecycle is standard.
[05:36] Priya: Slight tangent — our platform often needs deterministic reproducibility of results for debugging. If a fallback changed the model variant, we need a way to re-run the request against the original model. Is that possible?
[05:45] Ethan: Yes, you can pin the model version and rehydrate the exact request with token-level traces. We also preserve model hashes in the audit logs so you can replay.
[05:53] Jonas: Last technical question: how do KV cache and prefix caching behave during failovers? Do you lose warm cache state when traffic reroutes to a different region?
[06:01] Ethan: Good question. KV cache is region-local by default. We provide optional global KV sync for hot prefixes but it's eventually consistent; there is a warmup delta when switching regions. For strict consistency you'd want sticky routing, or to support a read-only cache fallback that uses embeddings+cache to approximate.
[06:17] Priya: That eventual consistency is a concern. We might prefer a model that serves degraded outputs but preserves critical step continuity.
[06:22] Samira: That's a tradeoff; many customers accept short-lived reduced QoS for continuity. We'll show several topology diagrams — sticky sessions, global replicated cache, and cached prefix fallbacks — in the POC documentation.
[06:33] Marta: Any legal/contractual limits around data residency? Our bioinformatics data must stay in- region for certain workflows.
[06:38] Samira: You can pin models and data to regions. Dedicated and Private give you stricter controls for data residency. We'll document options including geo-fencing and region pinning APIs.
[06:46] Jonas: What about testing scenarios for cascading failures — e.g., failover induces overload downstream and causes more failures. Do you offer circuit breakers?
[06:52] Ethan: Yes, we support circuit-breaker patterns at the service mesh layer and at the request routing layer. Policies allow you to implement exponential backoff, progressive throttling, and canary rollback if quality metrics degrade.
[07:02] Priya: For the POC timeline, we're aiming to pick a vendor by mid-April. Does that align with Redwood's ability to run a week-long pilot before then?
[07:10] Samira: Yes, we can schedule a 7-14 day pilot in late March/early April. We'll need your test prompts, traffic profile, and a stubbed client to run fault injection.
[07:18] Priya: I'll coordinate that. Jonas, can you lead on test prompts?
[07:21] Jonas: Yep, I'll prepare a set focusing on long-tail sequences and sensitive prompts that must be redacted.
[07:26] Marta: Important: we need an NDA addendum for running tests with sample PII.
[07:29] Samira: Noted. We'll send the standard addendum for review.
[07:33] Ethan: A quick demo note — during the POC we can enable the real-time dashboard and a synthetic traffic generator so you can observe failover and model switching in near real-time.
[07:41] Priya: Sounds good. A couple of small clarifications: can you send an example fallback DSL policy and a sample API header override?
[07:47] Ethan: Absolutely, I'll attach a sample policy and curl examples in the follow-up.
[07:51] Samira: To wrap, the action items are: share pricing and SLA examples, compliance pack, POC plan and failover topology, and set pilot dates. Anything else?
[07:59] Jonas: Please also include example telemetry dashboards and the exact list of metrics you'll collect.
[08:04] Marta: And send the SOC2 cert and KMS integration guide.
[08:07] Samira: Will do. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the materials and proposed POC dates.
[08:12] Priya: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:14] Ethan: Thanks all.
[08:16] Samira: Bye.

Notes on transcription: occasional misheard words (e.g., "KV cash" for KV cache), speaker overlap captured as short cuts, some proper nouns are approximate.
